Abstract
Distributed deep learning (DDL) applications generate heavy input/output (I/O) 
workloads that can create bottlenecks in high-performance computing (HPC) sys-
tems. Their optimal I/O configuration depends on factors such as access patterns, 
storage hardware, dataset size, and execution scale. This study proposes a system-
atic methodology for characterizing and optimizing I/O behavior in DDL applica-
tions, represented through the deep learning I/O benchmark (DLIO), and validated 
with the real DeepGalaxy application. We evaluate access modes, file formats, and 
Lustre file system configurations, demonstrating that stripe counts optimized for the 
access pattern and application scale can reduce I/O and execution times, achieving 
up to 18 GiB/s of bandwidth and a 5X increase in IOPS. HDF5 provides balanced 
performance, while TFRecord stands out in bandwidth-intensive scenarios. Shared 
access minimizes contention and improves scalability in multi-node executions. The 
results are consolidated into configuration guidelines that offer practical recommen-
dations for practitioners to tune DDL applications for efficient execution in HPC 
environments.

1  Introduction
Distributed deep learning (DDL) applications place unprecedented pressure on 
high-performance computing (HPC) storage systems. During training, massive 
datasets must be repeatedly accessed with high concurrency, leading to I/O bot-
tlenecks that can dominate execution time. In large-scale deployments, I/O has 
been shown to account for more than 90% of total training time when inefficient 
file formats are used [1], severely limiting scalability. Even in scientific work-
loads such as CANDLE and FRNN, where data volumes reach tens of terabytes,

and distributed training frameworks have drastically reduced compute time, I/O 
remains a critical barrier to end-to-end performance. This work aims to bridge 
I/O pattern characterization and configuration optimization in distributed deep 
learning workloads, providing a systematic understanding that links experimental 
observation with practical tuning strategies.
A key challenge is that deep learning workloads exhibit I/O behaviors that 
diverge significantly from traditional HPC applications. File formats, such as 
JPEG, HDF5, TFRecord, and NPZ, differ in metadata handling, compression, and 
support for parallel access, leading to widely varying throughput. Likewise, par-
allel file systems, such as Lustre, may either alleviate or exacerbate contention 
depending on chunking, striping, and access patterns. Misaligned configurations 
can result in severe performance degradation, with increased latency and over-
heads that grow worse as training scales to more nodes and processes.
This paper makes the following contributions:
Methodology for I/O characterization. We propose a systematic approach 
to identify significant I/O patterns in distributed deep learning applications, 
accounting for variability, randomness, frequency, and repetitive access. The 
methodology highlights how application parameters, dataset characteristics, and 
filesystem configurations impact parallel I/O performance.
Dual validation with synthetic and real workloads. We evaluate our methodol-
ogy using two complementary workloads: DLIO, which provides a configurable 
synthetic benchmark for controlled experiments, and DeepGalaxy, a real-world 
scientific application with complex and less predictable I/O behavior. This com-
bination ensures both systematic validation and practical relevance under realistic 
HPC constraints.
Quantitative evaluation of I/O configurations. We present a detailed analysis 
of how factors, such as access patterns, degree of parallelism, and Lustre strip-
ing, influence I/O time and training performance. Our experiments reveal that 
TFRecord achieves the highest bandwidth for large transfers, HDF5 balances 
scalability and memory efficiency, and shared access mode consistently reduces 
overhead compared to independent access mode.
Configuration guidelines for HPC environments. Based on experimental evi-
dence, we provide actionable recommendations organized by levels of the I/O 
software stack. These guidelines enable practitioners to select optimal file for-
mats, access modes, and filesystem parameters tailored to their application’s 
access pattern, dataset size, and scale.
Our experimental evaluation with DLIO and DeepGalaxy reveals that filesys-
tem and format choices have a decisive impact on I/O performance and training 
efficiency. Lustre with multiple OSTs improves I/O time in regular access pat-
terns, whereas misaligned striping in irregular workloads, such as DeepGalaxy, 
can increase contention and overhead. TFRecord achieves the highest bandwidth 
for large transfer sizes, while HDF5 provides a balanced trade-off between scal-
ability and memory usage. Additionally, shared access mode consistently outper-
forms independent access mode by reducing filesystem overhead.

2  Related work
Distributed deep learning systems face critical challenges in managing I/O perfor-
mance and optimization strategies. This section reviews key studies that provide 
frameworks and methodologies for addressing these challenges in HPC environ-
ments. The taxonomy proposed in Langer et  al. [3] categorizes distributed deep 
learning systems (DDLS) by their architectural principles, such as model versus data 
parallelism, and centralized versus decentralized optimization. This framework aids 
in understanding the fundamental design choices and their impact on distributed 
training performance.
Other works have focused on understanding and improving bandwidth usage in 
HPC I/O systems. The authors in [4] analyze the asynchronous I/O behavior of HPC 
applications and propose strategies to estimate bandwidth needs and perform I/O in 
the background, reducing the impact on computational phases. In [5], the authors 
propose AIO, a pipeline that automates the I/O optimization process using profil-
ing and adaptive strategies tailored to data-intensive applications. The authors in [6] 
present Tarazu, a framework for end-to-end adaptive I/O load balancing in paral-
lel file systems, which enables more efficient use of bandwidth in dynamic work-
loads. These approaches focus on system-level mechanisms and automation for I/O 
optimization, which complement our application-centric methodology by highlight-
ing the growing importance of I/O behavior modeling in DL workloads on HPC 
infrastructure.
The study in [7] addresses the behavior of I/O operations, proposing methods 
and techniques for managing different classes of I/O generated during deep learn-
ing tasks. Similarly, the analysis in [8] delves into the bottlenecks encountered dur-
ing the I/O processes in the training phase of machine learning models. This study 
includes examining access patterns and a performance model that elucidates the 
impact of various storage strategies on I/O efficiency.
Further contributions, such as the work in [9], explore the impact of machine 
learning techniques and hyperparameters on the overall performance of train-
ing tasks. These studies emphasize the complexities inherent in storage subsys-
tems, especially given the irregular I/O patterns observed in deep learning (DL)

In deep learning applications that train images, the choice of file format can sig-
nificantly impact I/O performance. The HDF5 (Hierarchical Data Format version 
5) is highly flexible and scalable, allowing large amounts of data to be stored in 
an organized hierarchical structure. With advanced features such as chunking and 
shared access across multiple processes, HDF5 is ideal for distributed comput-
ing environments. It also enables several instances to access different file portions 
simultaneously, improving I/O performance in parallel and distributed applications 
[15].
On the other hand, TFRecord is an optimized format for TensorFlow, specifically 
designed to store sequential data efficiently. It is recommended in large-scale train-
ing scenarios, as it facilitates prefetching and sequential reading of large volumes of 
data. TFRecord, optimized for batch processing and data distribution across multiple 
GPUs or compute nodes, significantly improves I/O speed in distributed architec-
tures [16].
Finally, the NPZ format, based on NumPy array compression, offers a simple 
solution for storing multiple arrays in a single compressed file. While space-efficient 
and easy to use in Python development environments, NPZ does not include the I/O 
optimizations provided by HDF5 and TFRecord. It is, therefore, more suitable for 
smaller or local projects where distributed processing or concurrent access is not 
required [17].
Our research distinguishes itself by performing I/O analysis of parallel datasets 
within DL applications operating in HPC environments. The main goal is to provide 
users with detailed and actionable insights into how specific elements of the applica-
tions, datasets, and system parameters can influence the performance of their deep 
learning applications. By clearly understanding how these factors interact, users can 
decide on the optimal configuration of their systems and applications, achieving 
superior performance in their DL applications within HPC contexts.
From a dual perspective, our approach combines the evaluation of a configur-
able synthetic tool (DLIO) with a real scientific application (DeepGalaxy), allow-
ing us to validate the methodology under both reproducible and practical conditions. 
Unlike previous studies, we present a detailed spatiotemporal analysis of I/O access 
patterns, comparing the impact of different file formats (HDF5, NPZ, TFRecord), 
access modes (shared vs. independent), and system-level parameters such as the 
number of Lustre stripes and the transfer size. Furthermore, we propose using a 
reduced set of system resources as a reference scenario, focusing on user-accessible

To validate the methodology, the DLIO and DeepGalaxy applications were 
selected to cover both synthetic and real scenarios of distributed deep learning 
workloads. The DLIO Benchmark [2] is a configurable tool designed to emulate 
typical I/O patterns in HPC environments. Its controlled environment allows the 
modification of parameters such as file format, number of processes, access mode, 
and transfer size, while aspects, such as the number of OSTs, are configured at the 
file system level. Its access pattern is sequential and predictable, making it ideal for 
validating each stage of the methodology under reproducible conditions. In contrast, 
DeepGalaxy [18] is a real scientific application for galaxy classification. It exhibits 
more complex access patterns influenced by the neural network design, paralleliza-
tion strategy, and data loading scheme. This less regular behavior enables the evalu-
ation of the practical applicability of the methodology in real-world contexts, where 
I/O bottlenecks may not be immediately apparent.
The combination of both applications, one synthetic and one real, ensures a com-
prehensive evaluation: DLIO supports the systematic analysis of I/O patterns, while 
DeepGalaxy demonstrates the practical utility of the proposed approach in real sci-
entific workflows on HPC systems. In the following, we detail each phase of the 
methodology.
The novelty of this methodology lies in its integrative nature: combining spati-
otemporal analysis of I/O patterns with empirical quantification of performance and 
prescriptive configuration guidelines. This ensures both analytical depth and practi-
cal applicability. While existing HPC I/O analysis efforts have mostly focused on 
characterization alone or on system-level optimizations, our methodology bridges 
these two perspectives by offering a systematic framework that not only describes 
I/O behaviors but also prescribes configuration strategies tailored to distributed deep 
learning workloads.
3.1  Characterization
The characterization phase identifies key elements to describe the application’s 
functionality, the dataset, computing system, and storage system, all of which can 
influence performance behavior.

cific requirements and challenges to tailor the application effectively.
After defining the tasks, selecting an appropriate software stack becomes essen-
tial. This includes choosing frameworks (e.g., TensorFlow [16], Horovod [20]), 
parallel programming languages, as well as libraries, which form the application’s

3.1.3  System
It is important to characterize the system because it allows you to understand what 
environment the application is running in, which includes knowing the resource 
limitations such as processing capacity, memory, and storage. This helps identify 
constraints that could affect the performance and efficiency of input/output (I/O) 
operations.
The system description provides an in-depth overview of the environment where 
the DDL application operates. In the case of this work, this environment is built on 
a HPC system designed to handle demanding computational tasks. We use the infra-

substantial memory resources and high-speed local storage, ensuring that the system 
is capable of efficiently managing large-scale DDL workloads.
In addition to the compute nodes, the system is interconnected through an Infini-
band HDR 100 network, which facilitates rapid communication between nodes, a 
critical factor in maintaining high performance across distributed computations.

cations. Designed for high-performance computing (HPC) environments, Lustre

3.2.2  Dataset
The dataset used to train the deep neural network is characterized by its size, quality,

The access mode defines how processes interact with the data: in multi-access, each

processes interact with the same file, coordinating I/O operations.

3.2.3  System
Configuring a high-performance computing (HPC) system for deep learning (DL) 
applications requires careful consideration of several critical parameters to ensure 
optimal performance.
•	 Processes and Nodes: The number of processes and nodes directly affects the 
distribution of the computational load across the cluster. While increasing the 
number of processes can enhance parallelism, careful tuning is required to mini-
mize communication overhead, especially in distributed DL environments [24]. 
Similarly, the number of nodes must balance computational demands with effi-
cient I/O operations.
•	 File System Selection: The choice of file system significantly affects data 
throughput, latency, and system efficiency. Parallel file systems and distributed 
file systems, such as Lustre, general parallel file system (GPFS), or BeeGFS, are 
commonly used for their ability to handle high-bandwidth data access, essential 
for DDL-intensive workloads [25]. Another widely used file system is the net-
work file system (NFS). NFS, a protocol developed by Sun Microsystems, ena-
bles distributed file storage across nodes, providing users with seamless access 
to remote files as if they were local [26, 27]. While widely adopted in high-
performance computing for its simplicity and flexibility, NFS performance can 
be constrained by network latency and concurrency challenges under intensive 
workloads.
•	 Lustre-Specific Configurations: For parallel file systems like Lustre, stripe size 
and stripe count are key configuration parameters.
–	 Stripe Size: Defines the data block size written to each disk. Optimizing this 
parameter improves performance for sequential and random workloads [28].
–	 Data Servers: Denotes the number of data servers (DS) or object storage tar-
gets (OSTs) in Lustre used for file storage. While increasing the number of 
stripes can enhance performance, it may also introduce management overhead 
[29, 30].
•	 Memory Allocation: Sufficient memory allocation is essential to prevent per-
formance bottlenecks during data processing. The memory requirements depend 
on the dataset size and model complexity, and optimizing memory use ensures 
smooth application execution.
For this study, we used the following system configuration:
•	 File System Configuration. Lustre parallel file system was selected for its high-
throughput capabilities. Key configurations included:
–	 Stripe Size: A 1 MiB stripe size (1,048,576 bytes) was selected to balance 
performance for large sequential data operations.
–	 Stripe Count: Configurations were tested with 1, 2, 4, 8, and 12 OSTs, align-
ing the stripe count with the number of nodes to ensure efficient data distribu-

The instrumentation and monitoring framework for the DeepGalaxy application is

These metrics include system latency, data transfer rates, and resource utilization,

tion, and the Shared, Reload and Shuffle mode (m>0), which periodically reloads 
and redistributes data to improve diversity at the potential cost of higher latency.
Real-time monitoring scripts were deployed to log metrics such as I/O operations, 
latency, and data transfer rates under different configurations. This setup enables a 
comprehensive analysis of data flow patterns, helping to identify the optimal con-

insights are instrumental in fine-tuning DeepGalaxy’s data loading strategies to min-
imize delays and bottlenecks, ensuring robust performance even in large-scale dis-

4.7  Comparative analysis of I/O patterns: DLIO vs. DeepGalaxy
The comparative study between DLIO and DeepGalaxy reveals fundamental dif-

and strided behaviors are clearly identifiable, with constant offsets and predictable 
request sizes determined by user-specified parameters (e.g., record length, trans-
fer size, and access mode). This regularity produces reproducible traces with low 
variance across processes, enabling systematic evaluation of scalability effects and

alignments with Lustre striping, and heterogeneous request sizes, often below 30 
KiB. Temporal patterns also differ: instead of the constant inter-request intervals 
observed in DLIO, DeepGalaxy alternates between bursts of intensive I/O and idle 
phases corresponding to computation. At larger scales, these irregularities gener-

6  Configuration guidelines
Based on the experimental evaluation of the DeepGalaxy application on the Lustre 
file system, the following recommendations are proposed to optimize I/O efficiency 
and scalability:
•	 Stripe Count (OSTs): In low-parallelism scenarios (1 node, up to 4 processes), 
increasing the stripe count generally improves I/O performance by distributing 
data across multiple OSTs, leading to better bandwidth utilization and higher 
IOPS. However, in high-parallelism configurations, the gains become less 
consistent, with performance improvements not scaling proportionally to the 
increase in OSTs. This behavior is closely related to the irregular I/O access pat-
tern of DeepGalaxy, where nonuniform and scattered reads can limit the benefits 
of wider data striping. In such cases, additional OSTs may introduce synchroni-
zation overhead and intensify metadata contention, offsetting the expected per-
formance gains beyond a moderate stripe count.
•	 Access Mode:
–	 Shared access mode: Generally delivers better performance than Shared 
(reload+shuffle), as the absence of additional reloading/shuffling minimizes 
metadata activity and OST contention, which are aggravated by irregular 
access patterns.
–	 Shared (reload+shuffle): Randomized reloading and shuffling operations 
amplify the coordination costs introduced by higher stripe counts. For work-
loads combining this mode with an irregular base pattern, a single OST is 
often preferable to avoid performance degradation.
•	 Parallelism scaling: Increasing the number of nodes and processes reduces I/O 
time and improves scalability up to a point. However, with DeepGalaxy’s irregu-
lar access, the benefits plateau at higher levels of concurrency, as synchroniza-

the nonuniform I/O distribution.
6.1  Interpretation and use of the configuration guidance table
Table 13 summarizes practical configuration guidelines derived from the experimen-
tal results and performance patterns observed in our analysis of the DLIO Bench-
mark and DeepGalaxy applications. Organized according to the layers of the deep 
learning I/O software stack from the application level to the object storage system 
(Lustre), the table highlights common performance issues, the corresponding system 
or application factors contributing to them, and recommended strategies to mitigate 
their impact. These recommendations are based on the specific experimental con-
figurations evaluated in this study, which primarily involve image-based distributed 
deep learning workloads. While some strategies may apply to other domains, the 
values and tuning suggestions should be interpreted as practical guidelines rather 
than universal rules. Future work will extend this analysis to a broader range of 
application types with diverse I/O patterns.
At the application level, issues, such as high I/O time or poor scalability, may 
arise due to limited parallelism, small batch sizes, or inefficient chunking strategies. 
Our experiments with a batch size of 64 demonstrate reduced latency and improved 
throughput. These results are consistent with prior studies showing that larger batch 
sizes can further enhance scalability and training efficiency in distributed deep 
learning workloads. In particular, [34] demonstrated that ResNet50 can be trained 
on ImageNet with minibatches of up to 8192 images in just one hour without loss 
of accuracy. Similarly, [35] scaled ImageNet training to batch sizes as large as 32k 
using the LARS algorithm, also preserving accuracy [1,2]. Likewise, using shared 
HDF5 files or large chunks helps minimize metadata overhead caused by numerous 
small files.
The domain-specific wrapper layer reflects choices related to file formats and 
data preparation. Low bandwidth may stem from the use of low-throughput formats 
or small transfer sizes (e.g., 256 KiB), for which optimized formats like HDF5 or 
TFRecord, along with larger transfer sizes ( >= 1 MiB), are recommended.

In the DL I/O middleware and low-level middleware layers, fragmented or mis-
aligned transfers and irregular access patterns (including unbalanced OST usage) 
increase I/O time and reduce bandwidth. Strategies such as grouping read/write 
operations, adjusting chunk sizes, and aligning access patterns with striping configu-
rations can significantly reduce these overheads.
At the file system and object store (Lustre) layers, bottlenecks in IOPS and 
bandwidth are frequently linked to small chunks, high-frequency access, concur-
rent access to a single OST, or nonuniform OST usage caused by irregular patterns. 
Improvements include increasing the OST count, optimizing chunking strategies 
(e.g., from 5 × 64 to 5 ×128), and configuring striping to match the node/process lay-
out. While in highly irregular patterns, a lower OST count may be preferable.
These recommendations aim to bridge the gap between raw experimental data 
and actionable configuration decisions, enabling users and system administrators 
to adapt their setups to the specific I/O characteristics of DDL applications. While 
these findings are based on the workloads studied in this paper, the patterns observed 
are representative of many common deep learning scenarios. These guidelines are 
intended to be applicable to other distributed deep learning workloads that exhibit 
similar I/O patterns and scalability behaviors, and can guide efficient configuration 
in comparable HPC environments.
7  Conclusions
This study presents a systematic methodology to analyze I/O behavior in distributed 
deep learning applications, using the DLIO benchmark and the DeepGalaxy appli-
cation as case studies. By varying configuration parameters such as access modes 
and dataset formats, the results show how these factors influence I/O patterns and 
overall performance. In particular, Lustre file systems configured with multiple 
object storage targets (OSTs) and tuned parameters achieved improvements in I/O 
time, bandwidth, and execution efficiency. These benefits are especially significant 
when the access pattern is regular and well aligned with the striping strategy, as this 
enables a more uniform utilization of OST capacity. However, for irregular or highly 
fragmented patterns, increasing the stripe count can lead to metadata overhead 
and greater pressure on the coordination subsystem, reducing the expected benefit. 
Therefore, scalability has practical limits, as increasing the stripe count can improve 
data distribution and reduce contention when concurrency is low or moderate. Still, 
beyond a certain point, the extra coordination and metadata handling can outweigh 
the benefits, resulting in little or no gain in bandwidth or IOPS. For this reason, the 
stripe count should be chosen according to the application’s access pattern, dataset 
size, and target scale.
Access mode and file format were also found to be key performance factors. In 
the DeepGalaxy application, shared access reduced I/O contention and improved run 
times, while independent access increased overhead, revealing trade-offs between 
isolated file handling and shared resource efficiency. Regarding file formats, HDF5 
provided a balanced compromise between scalability and memory efficiency,

Scalability analysis confirmed that increasing the number of processes and nodes 
consistently reduced I/O and execution times, demonstrating the benefits of paral-
lelism. Nonetheless, higher concurrency increased total memory usage, underscor-
ing the need for advanced memory management strategies to sustain performance 
and prevent bottlenecks. These findings are consolidated in the final phase of our 
methodology, configuration guidelines, which distills the observed behaviors into 
actionable recommendations structured by levels of the I/O software stack, enabling 
practitioners to translate performance trends into optimal parameter choices for their 
workloads and infrastructure.
The methodology is adaptable to other applications, enabling users to character-
ize their own I/O patterns and make informed configuration decisions. The experi-
ments shown here represent a selected subset chosen for clarity; however, a broader 
set of tests was performed during the study, all following the same methodology and 
confirming the observed trends. This makes the approach particularly useful in real 
HPC environments, where application behavior and system constraints vary signifi-
cantly depending on the use case.
Future work will extend the analysis to workloads with different access patterns, 
such as natural language processing (NLP) tasks, scientific simulations, and appli-
cations involving unstructured or semi-structured data, allowing broader validation 
of the methodology and comparisons between optimal configurations for different 
domains.

Abstract: Distributed deep learning (DDL) applications generate heavy input/output (I/O) workloads that can create bottlenecks in high-performance computing (HPC) sys- tems. Their optimal I/O configuration depends on factors such as access patterns, storage hardware, dataset size, and execution scale. This study proposes a system- atic methodology for characterizing and optimizing I/O behavior in DDL applica- tions, represented through the deep learning I/O benchmark (DLIO), and validated with the real DeepGalaxy application. We evaluate access modes, file formats, and Lustre file system configurations, demonstrating that stripe counts optimized for the access pattern and application scale can reduce I/O and execution times, achieving up to 18 GiB/s of bandwidth and a 5X increase in IOPS. HDF5 provides balanced performance, while TFRecord stands out in bandwidth-intensive scenarios. Shared access minimizes contention and improves scalability in multi-node executions. The results are consolidated into configuration guidelines that offer practical recommen- dations for practitioners to tune DDL applications for efficient execution in HPC environments.
